title: Tibo's 12-step playbook for taking SaaS apps to $100K MRR
summary: Tibo walks through the repeatable 12-step process behind four SaaS apps passing $100K MRR. The core idea: ship MVPs in days, talk daily to relevant users until retention is sticky, then go broad on distribution and double down on one or two channels. He also explains why he runs a portfolio of products.

principles.text: Build the MVP in days or weeks using shortcuts like no-code and boilerplates, since most ideas fail.
principles.quote: You will have a 90% failure rate. It's same for me, it's the same for a lot of people that I know.

principles.text: Get feedback only from 5-10 people who are your real target audience; irrelevant feedback, good or bad, is worthless.
principles.quote: If the person is not relevant, like there is absolutely no point in listening to this feedback, either positive or negative.

principles.text: Route support to your personal DMs and fix issues in minutes until a product hits $10K/month; fast responsiveness creates customers for life.
principles.quote: until each product is making 10 K per month in revenue, the supports link on each software is directing people to my Twitter DMs.

principles.text: Be the user of your own product to build features that solve real user problems and understand the core pain.
principles.quote: I'm being the user of my own products. And by doing that, I'm 10 times more relevant with understanding the core problem and giving a proper solution.

principles.text: Don't scale acquisition before retention; iterate until users can't live without it, and treat complaints as a sign of commitment.
principles.quote: If you go abroad, like if you focus on acquisition and at the same time have a low retention, you will spend a lot of energy pushing people to your software, and 99% of those people are going to flow away directly after trying your software.

principles.text: Scale with SEO, ads and affiliates once you have stickiness, then go all in on the one or two channels that work and kill the rest.
principles.quote: in the end, my experience is for each software, growth is pretty much about one or two acquisition channels. Those two acquisition channels, I'm going all in on them.
